title: What "8000W" Really Means on a Blender in Ghana
excerpt: Almost every blender sold in Ghana claims 4500W or 8000W. On a Ghanaian socket, both numbers are physically impossible. Here is the arithmetic, and the real number.
content:
Quick answer. No blender plugged into a Ghanaian wall socket can draw 8000W, or 4500W. A Type G socket delivers at most 2,990W and a Type D at most 1,380W. The number on the box is a peak marketing figure. Real continuous draw on a typical 2L commercial blender is around 600W, which costs about GHS 6.11 a month to run.

The arithmetic anyone can check

Ghana's mains supply is 230 volts. Power is volts multiplied by amps. The two domestic socket types set a hard ceiling:

SocketRated ampsMaximum deliverable power
Type G (the rectangular three pin)13A230 x 13 = 2,990W
Type D (the round three pin)6A230 x 6 = 1,380W

An 8000W load would need 34.8 amps, which is 2.7 times what a Type G socket can supply and 5.8 times a Type D. The fuse in the plug blows long before the motor ever sees that power. A 4500W claim needs 19.6 amps and fails the same test.

So why is the number on the box?

It is a peak or stall figure: the instantaneous surge at motor startup, or the theoretical maximum the windings could momentarily survive. It is not what the motor draws while blending your pepper. The same trick inflates horsepower claims on premium blender brands worldwide. One horsepower is 746 watts, so treat these labels as marketing units rather than electrical ones.

What it actually costs you to run

At the PURC residential rate of GHS 2.04 per kWh, effective 1 July 2026, ten minutes of blending a day comes to:

Real continuous drawkWh per monthCost per month
300W1.5GHS 3.06
600W (typical 2L commercial)3.0GHS 6.11
800W4.0GHS 8.15
1200W6.0GHS 12.23

Here is the part that should change how you shop: the blender, the appliance with the scariest number on the box, is one of the cheapest things in your kitchen to run. The quiet ones are the expensive ones. A double burner hot plate at typical use costs about GHS 91.69 a month.

What to look at instead of the wattage

Jar size for your family, whether it comes with a genuine dry mill if you grind grains and spices, blade metal, and whether the seller holds local stock so a warranty claim has somewhere to go. Every blender we sell states its realistic draw class, its running cost at the current tariff, and its price verified for the current month.

Sources and working: PURC Q2 2026 tariff decision plus the 3.49 per cent increase effective 1 July 2026; Ghana mains 230V; socket ratings per the Type G (13A) and Type D (6A) standards. Cost formula: watts / 1000 x hours per day x 30 x rate.

title: What 30,000mAh Really Delivers to Your Phone
excerpt: A power bank never delivers its advertised mAh. The physics is settled and the arithmetic is simple. Here is the real number, and how many charges you actually get.
content:
Quick answer. A "30,000mAh" power bank delivers roughly 15,500 to 18,900mAh to your phone, about three to four full charges of a typical 5,000mAh battery, not six. This is true of every brand at every price. The cells store charge at 3.7 volts, your phone receives it at 5 volts, and the conversion between them loses energy as heat.

The formula

Energy is conserved in watt hours, not milliamp hours. The advertised mAh is measured at the cell voltage, and delivery happens at USB voltage:

Real mAh at 5V = (3.7 x advertised mAh x efficiency) / 5.0

Quality units convert at about 85 per cent efficiency. Budget units, which is most of what sells in Accra, run nearer 70 per cent.

AdvertisedStored energyReal at 5V (budget)Real at 5V (quality)
10,000mAh37.0 Wh5,180mAh6,290mAh
20,000mAh74.0 Wh10,360mAh12,580mAh
30,000mAh111.0 Wh15,540mAh18,870mAh

The industry already admits this

Anker publishes the same arithmetic for its own products, quoting roughly 82 per cent efficiency and a "rated capacity" near 6,068mAh on a 10,000mAh bank. The information is not hidden. It is just never said at the point of sale in Ghana.

How many charges you actually get

Divide the real delivered figure by your phone's battery. A 5,000mAh phone gets about one full charge from a 10,000mAh bank, two from a 20,000mAh, and three to four from a 30,000mAh. If a listing promises six charges from 30,000mAh, the seller has not done the arithmetic, or hopes you will not.

One more thing before you fly

Airlines generally cap carry-on batteries at 100Wh without approval. A 30,000mAh unit stores about 111Wh, over that line. Up to 20,000mAh (74Wh) travels without questions.

Why we tell you this

Because you already know your power bank underdelivers. You have owned one. We would rather be the shop that explains why, with the working on the page, than the fifth listing shouting a number physics does not permit. Every power bank we sell states its honest charge count, and its price is verified for the current month.

title: Why A GHS 280 Blender Grinds Pepper Better Than A GHS 900 One
excerpt: The expensive blender on the shelf is built for smoothies. Ghanaian pepper needs the opposite thing. Here is the mechanism, and what it means for what you should buy.
content:
Quick answer. Grinding pepper needs turning force at low speed, not blade speed. Cheap Ghanaian-market blenders use high-torque motors with narrow, steep jars, which is exactly right for pepper, ginger and groundnut. Expensive smoothie blenders optimise for speed in a wide jar, which whips soft fruit beautifully and stalls on a dry chilli. This is why a GHS 280 machine out-grinds a GHS 900 one on the job you actually do.

The moment this matters

It is six in the morning. You have half a bowl of dried pepper, ginger, garlic and a little onion, and you want it ground before the children wake. You switch on, the motor screams, and the pepper sits at the top of the jar spinning around the blade without ever meeting it. You add water you did not want to add. That is not a bad blender. That is a blender built for a different job.

Torque and speed are not the same thing

Every motor trades one for the other. Speed is how fast the blade spins. Torque is how hard it keeps spinning when something resists it.

Soft fruit offers almost no resistance, so a smoothie machine can chase speed. Dried pepper, ginger and groundnut are hard and dry. They resist. The moment a high-speed low-torque blade meets them it slows, and a slowing blade cannot cut. You hear it as the motor note dropping, then you hear it rise again as the blade spins free in a pocket of air it has carved for itself.

A high-torque motor does the opposite. It turns slower and refuses to be stopped. It keeps chewing.

The jar matters as much as the motor

This is the part almost nobody is told. A smoothie jar is wide at the base so liquid can circulate. A grinding jar is narrow and steep, so gravity keeps feeding dry material back down onto the blade instead of letting it climb the walls.

Look at the two jars side by side on the shelf. The one that looks cheap and narrow is the one that will grind your pepper dry, without added water, which is what you want if you are making shito or storing a batch.

The number to look at instead of wattage

The wattage printed on the box is a peak marketing figure. We have covered why in a separate piece: a Ghanaian 13A socket can deliver at most 2,990W, so any blender claiming 4500W or 8000W is quoting something that cannot physically happen in your kitchen.

What to look at instead:

  • Jar shape. Narrow and steep for dry grinding. Wide for drinks.
  • A separate dry mill. The small cup with the flat blade. If it has one, it is built with grinding in mind.
  • The coupling. The part joining motor to jar. Metal outlasts plastic by years on a machine used daily.
  • Weight. A heavier base usually means more copper in the motor, which usually means more torque.

What we found on the ground

In July 2026 we priced 2L commercial-style blenders with a dry mill across Accra dealers. The working range was GHS 280 to GHS 340. The same shelves carried imported smoothie machines from GHS 850 upward that grind soft fruit better and dry pepper worse.

If your kitchen mostly makes pepper, shito, ginger and groundnut, the cheaper machine is not a compromise. It is the correct tool, and you keep the difference.

Who should buy which

Buy the commercial-style grinder if you cook Ghanaian food daily, make shito in batches, or sell food. It will grind dry, and the metal coupling survives daily use.

Buy the smoothie machine if you mainly make drinks, smoothies and soups, and grind pepper only occasionally with a little water.

Check it before you pay

When the rider reaches you, before any money changes hands: lift the base and feel the weight, turn the jar to check the coupling is metal and seats firmly, and run it empty for five seconds to hear whether the motor note is steady. If anything is not as described, do not pay. That is the whole point of pay on delivery.

See the blenders we stock, each with the real jar type and coupling material stated. Pay on delivery in Accra, same day where we can.

title: How Long A Rechargeable Fan Really Runs When The Light Goes
excerpt: Two fans claim the same battery and one dies at 2am while the other is still turning at dawn. The difference is the motor, not the battery. Here are the real hours.
content:
Quick answer. Two rechargeable fans with the same advertised battery can differ by three times in real runtime, because runtime is set by how much current the motor draws, not by the battery alone. A brushless motor on speed one will run most of the night. A cheap brushed motor on speed three will not reach 2am. Ask for the motor type and the current draw, not just the mAh.

The moment this matters

Eleven at night, the light goes, and the room is already warm. The children are asleep. You switch the fan to the speed that actually moves air, and you go to bed hoping. At two in the morning somebody is awake and crying because the fan stopped an hour ago. You bought a fan advertised at 20,000mAh. It should have lasted. It did not.

Runtime is a division, and most people are only told the top half

The arithmetic is simple and nobody prints it on the box:

Hours = battery capacity divided by current draw.

The box gives you the capacity. It almost never gives you the draw. So you are handed the numerator and asked to guess the denominator, and the denominator is where all the variation lives.

A 16 inch rechargeable fan with a cheap brushed motor typically pulls around 20 to 26 watts on its top speed. The same size fan with a brushless DC motor pulls roughly 8 to 12 watts for a similar amount of air. Same battery, and one of them empties it in less than half the time.

What we measured

In July 2026 we ran two 16 inch rechargeable fans of the same claimed 20,000mAh capacity from full charge until they stopped, in a room at normal Accra night temperature.

FanSpeed 1Speed 3
Brushed motorabout 7 hoursabout 3 hours 20 minutes
Brushless DC motorabout 14 hoursabout 6 hours 30 minutes

The brushless fan on speed one covered a full night with hours to spare. The brushed fan on speed three did not reach 2am, which is exactly the failure people describe.

Three things that decide your real hours

  • Motor type. Brushless DC is the single biggest factor. It is usually stated as "BLDC" or "DC motor" and it is worth paying for.
  • The speed you actually use. Dropping from speed three to speed one roughly doubles your night. Most rooms only need speed one once the air is moving.
  • Whether the light is on. The built-in LED panel on many of these fans is not free. Running it all night can cost you an hour or more.

The honest limitation

A rechargeable fan is a fan, not an inverter. It will not run a fridge, and it will not run all night on top speed no matter what the box says. If you need a whole room cooled through a long outage, you are looking at a different class of product and a different budget. We would rather tell you that now than sell you a disappointment.

What to ask before you buy

Ask three questions and you cannot go far wrong: is the motor brushless, what is the runtime on speed one, and does that figure include the light. If a seller cannot answer, they have not measured it.

Check it before you pay

At your door, before money: check the fan arrives charged enough to switch on, run it on each speed, and listen. A brushless motor is noticeably quieter and steadier. If it rattles or the speeds barely differ, do not pay.

See the rechargeable fans we stock, each listed with its motor type and the runtime we measured, not the runtime on the box. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: How To Check An Appliance At Your Door Before You Pay
excerpt: The rider is standing there. You have maybe two minutes. Here is exactly what to look at, in order, so you never pay for the wrong thing.
content:
Quick answer. You have about two minutes at the door and four checks that matter: the box seal, the plug and cable, the item against what you were told, and a five second power test. Do them in that order. If any one fails, do not pay. Pay on delivery only protects you if you actually use it.

The moment this matters

The rider calls from the gate. You come out, he hands you a box, and there is a small social pressure to just pay and go back inside. That pressure is exactly what a careless seller relies on. Two minutes of checking is the difference between a good purchase and a thing you regret for two years.

The four checks, in order

1. The box and the seal, ten seconds

Look for a factory seal, not tape that has been reapplied. Look for crushing at the corners. A resealed box does not automatically mean a bad item, but it means you check the contents harder before deciding.

2. The plug and cable, twenty seconds

This one is Ghana specific and it catches a lot of people. Your wall socket is Type G, the rectangular three pin. Anything arriving with a two pin European plug was built for a different market and will need an adapter, which is a fire risk on a heat appliance drawing real current.

Then run the cable through your fingers from plug to body. You are feeling for a joint, a lump of tape, or a section that feels thinner. A repaired cable on a new item means it is not new.

3. The item against what you were told, forty seconds

Take out your phone and read back the message. Model, size, capacity, colour, what was included. Check each one against the thing in your hands. A 1.8L kettle is not a 2L kettle. A blender that was described with a dry mill should have the dry mill cup in the box.

This is why we put the exact specification in the WhatsApp message rather than a vague product name. It gives you something to check against.

4. The five second power test, thirty seconds

Plug it in and switch it on. Do not run a kettle dry or a blender loaded, just prove it powers up and the motor or element responds.

  • Motors should start smoothly and settle to a steady note. A rattle or a note that wanders means a bearing or an unbalanced fan.
  • Heating elements should draw immediately. On a kettle you hear the water note begin within a few seconds.
  • Batteries should show a charge indicator. A rechargeable fan or lamp that arrives completely flat cannot be tested, so treat that as a reason to wait.

The four sentences that make this easy

Most people find the checking socially awkward rather than difficult. So use plain words and stay friendly. "Let me just open it small." "Let me check the plug." "Let me put it on for a second." "This one is not what we agreed, so I will not take it today."

A rider carrying a genuine item has no problem with any of that. Reluctance is itself information.

What we do differently, and why

We send the full specification in the order message on purpose, so you have a written thing to check against at the door. We deliver before we take money, so the risk sits with us and not with you. And if the item is not what we said, you do not pay and the rider takes it back. No argument, no deposit lost.

That policy costs us money on the rare occasions it happens. It is worth it, because the alternative is a market where nobody trusts anybody and everybody pays a little more to cover the risk.

One thing to avoid

Do not pay in advance for a discount. A price that is only available if you send money first is not a discount. It is the whole risk moving from the seller to you, priced at a few cedis.

See exactly how ordering works with us, or browse what we stock. You check it, then you pay the rider. Never the other way round.

title: Why Some Electric Kettles Rust Within A Year And Others Never Do
excerpt: Two kettles both say stainless steel. One is spotted with rust by the following harmattan. The difference is a number nobody prints on the box.
content:
Quick answer. "Stainless steel" is a family, not a grade. Kettles built with 201 grade steel corrode in a year or two in a humid kitchen. Kettles built with 304 grade last many years. The grade is rarely printed, so you judge it by the magnet test, the weld line and the weight.

The moment this matters

You reach for the kettle one morning and there is a rust bloom around the base of the element, or a brown speckle inside the spout. The kettle is fifteen months old. You did nothing wrong. You simply bought a grade of steel that was never going to survive a Ghanaian kitchen.

What the grades actually mean

Stainless steel resists rust because of chromium, and it resists it much better with nickel added. The two grades you meet on kettles:

GradeNickelBehaviour in a humid kitchen
201about 1%Cheaper. Corrodes at welds and around the element within one to two years.
304about 8%Standard for food equipment. Resists pitting for many years.

Nickel is the expensive ingredient, which is exactly why the cheaper kettle uses less of it. The saving is real and so is the consequence.

Three ways to tell them apart on the spot

  • The magnet test. 304 is essentially non-magnetic, so a fridge magnet slides off or clings very weakly. 201 has enough magnetic response that a magnet holds noticeably. This is not a laboratory test and cold working can affect it, but as a quick check at the door it is genuinely useful.
  • The weld line inside. Look down into the body at the vertical seam. A clean, even, barely visible weld suggests better manufacturing throughout. A rough, discoloured or pitted seam is where rust will start.
  • Weight. Pick up two kettles of the same capacity. The heavier one usually has thicker steel, which resists both corrosion and denting.

Why the water tastes different

The other thing people notice and rarely explain: a metallic taste in the first cup. That is usually not the steel body at all, it is an exposed heating element, the coil you can see sitting in the water. Exposed elements scale up quickly in hard water and shed that scale into your tea.

A concealed element, where the base is a flat plate and you see no coil, keeps the metal out of the water, descales far more easily, and is the single feature most worth paying a little more for.

What this costs in Accra

In July 2026 the working range we found across Accra dealers for a 1.8L to 2L kettle:

  • Plastic body, exposed element: GHS 90 to 120
  • 201 grade steel, exposed element: GHS 110 to 150
  • 304 grade steel, concealed element: GHS 160 to 230

The gap between the cheapest and the best here is roughly GHS 100. Spread over the extra years you get, it is the easiest upgrade decision in the whole kitchen.

Keeping it alive either way

Whatever grade you own, empty it after use rather than leaving water standing, and descale it monthly with vinegar or lime. Standing water plus an exposed element is how a kettle dies early.

Check it before you pay

At the door: look inside for a concealed flat base rather than a visible coil, run the magnet over the body, check the seam, and switch it on for five seconds to hear the element engage. If the body is magnetic and the element is exposed and you were told it was 304 with a concealed base, do not pay.

See the kettles we stock, with the element type stated on every one. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: Dry Iron Or Steam Iron For Kente, Lace And Everyday Clothes
excerpt: Steam is not automatically better. On kente, lace and most synthetics it is the thing that ruins them. Here is which iron suits which cloth.
content:
Quick answer. Steam relaxes fibres by wetting them, which is exactly right for cotton and linen and exactly wrong for kente, lace and most synthetics. For a Ghanaian wardrobe that mixes traditional cloth with office shirts, a dry iron plus a damp pressing cloth is the safer tool. Buy steam only if you press cotton shirts daily.

The moment this matters

You have a function on Saturday. The cloth has been folded for months and it needs pressing. You reach for the steam iron because steam sounds gentler, and you leave a shine on the fabric that will not come out. That mark is heat plus moisture plus pressure on threads that cannot take all three at once.

What steam actually does

Steam does not clean or protect. It wets the fibre so it becomes temporarily flexible, then the plate flattens it and it dries in the new shape. On cotton and linen, which are strong when wet, that is ideal and it is why a steam iron makes a shirt collar crisp in one pass.

On other fibres the same mechanism causes harm:

  • Kente and woven traditional cloth. The threads are tightly interlaced and often contain rayon or silk-like yarns. Wet heat plus pressure flattens the weave's texture and leaves a permanent sheen.
  • Lace. The open structure means the plate presses directly on individual threads with no cloth to spread the load. Steam softens them first, so they crush.
  • Polyester and most synthetics. These do not absorb water, they melt. Steam adds no benefit and the temperature needed to make steam is often above what the fibre tolerates.

The temperatures that matter

Irons hide this behind dots on a dial, which is why so many garments get damaged. In plain numbers:

SettingRoughlySafe for
One dot110 CNylon, acetate, most synthetics
Two dots150 CPolyester, silk, wool blends
Three dots200 CCotton, linen

Polyester begins to soften around 160 C. A three dot setting is comfortably past that, which is how a shirt gets a shiny patch in one careless pass.

The technique that protects traditional cloth

Use a dry iron on two dots, and put a thin cotton cloth between the plate and the garment. Dampen that pressing cloth, not the garment. You get controlled moisture spread evenly, the plate never touches the fibres directly, and the weave keeps its texture. This is how tailors do it and it costs nothing.

Which to buy

Dry iron if your wardrobe is mixed, if you own kente or lace, if you share the iron with people who will not check the dial, or if you want the simplest thing that lasts. Fewer parts, no water tank to scale up, and in a hard water area that matters.

Steam iron if you press cotton shirts most days and want speed. Buy one with a removable tank and descale it, because scale is what kills them.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026, across Accra dealers: a 1200W dry iron with a non-stick sole plate ran GHS 150 to 200. A comparable steam iron ran GHS 220 to 320. The dry iron is both cheaper and, for most Ghanaian wardrobes, the more suitable tool. That is not a compromise, it is a better match.

Check it before you pay

At the door: run a finger over the sole plate feeling for roughness or a nick, which will snag cloth. Switch it on and let it warm for thirty seconds to confirm the element and thermostat respond. Check the cable where it meets the body for a joint or tape.

See the irons we stock, with the sole plate type and wattage stated. Pay on delivery in Accra.

title: Why Barbers Replace Blades, Not Clippers
excerpt: A clipper that pulls hair is almost never a dead motor. It is a dulled or misaligned blade, and that is a cheap fix most owners never make.
content:
Quick answer. The blade does the cutting and the motor only turns it, so blades wear out long before motors do. A clipper that pulls hair usually needs a blade replaced or realigned, not throwing away. Working barbers change blades every few months and keep the same clipper for years, which is why they buy for motor quality and blade availability, not for the accessory count in the box.

The moment this matters

You are halfway through a cut and the clipper starts pulling instead of cutting. The client winces. You push harder, which makes it worse. Most people conclude the clipper has died and buy another one. It has not died. Two cutting edges have gone slightly blunt, or drifted out of alignment by a fraction of a millimetre.

How a clipper actually cuts

A clipper is a pair of scissors repeated forty or so times across a comb, operating a few thousand times a minute. There is a fixed lower blade and a moving upper blade. Hair enters between the teeth and is sheared where the two edges cross.

Two things stop that shear working:

  • Dullness. The edges round over with use. A rounded edge folds hair instead of cutting it, and folded hair is what you feel as a pull.
  • Alignment. The moving blade should sit slightly back from the fixed blade, commonly a fraction under half a millimetre. Too far forward and it catches skin. Too far back and hair is not gripped at all. Dropping a clipper is the usual cause.

Neither of those is a motor problem, which is why replacing the whole machine is usually the expensive way to solve a cheap fault.

What a working barber does

Ask around any shop in Accra and the routine is consistent: oil the blade at the start and end of every day, brush the hair out of the teeth after each client, and replace the blade set when cutting starts to drag rather than waiting for it to fail. On a busy chair that is every few months. The clipper body itself lasts years.

It follows that the two things worth paying for are a motor that holds its speed under load, and a blade that is easy to buy again locally. A clipper with a superb motor and a blade nobody stocks in Ghana is a clipper with an expiry date.

The three motor types

MotorCharacterBest for
MagneticCheapest, noisy, loses speed in thick hairOccasional home use
PivotSlower blade, much more cutting forceThick and coarse hair, wet cutting
RotarySteady speed under load, quieter, usually cordlessProfessional all-day use

For dense African hair, force matters more than blade speed, which is why pivot and rotary machines dominate professional shops and magnetic ones mostly sit in bathrooms.

What this costs in Accra

July 2026 across Accra dealers: a rechargeable metal-body clipper suitable for daily home use ran GHS 95 to 180. Professional rotary machines ran GHS 350 upward. A replacement blade set for a common model ran GHS 35 to 60, which is the number most owners never learn and the reason so many working clippers get discarded.

Making yours last

  • Oil the blade before and after every session. Two drops across the teeth, run it for ten seconds, wipe the excess.
  • Brush hair out of the teeth. Trapped hair holds moisture and moisture rusts the edges.
  • Do not run a cordless clipper flat every time. Lithium cells last longer topped up than emptied.
  • If it starts pulling, replace the blade before you replace the clipper.

Check it before you pay

At the door: run it and listen for a steady note rather than a rattle. Look along the blade edge to confirm the moving blade sits slightly behind the fixed one and the teeth line up. Confirm the charging cable and any guards described are actually in the box.

title: Your First Place In Accra: The Seven Things You Actually Need
excerpt: Moving into your own place, the temptation is to buy everything at once. Here is the honest short list, what each costs now, and what can wait.
content:
Quick answer. Seven items cover cooking, light, cooling and laundry for a first place in Accra, and in July 2026 they came to roughly GHS 1,150 to 1,500 across Accra dealers. Everything else can wait a month without you suffering. Buy the light and the fan first, because an outage on your first night is a miserable introduction to independence.

The moment this matters

You have the keys. The room echoes. You have some money but not unlimited money, and everybody is telling you a different thing to buy first. The mistake almost everyone makes is buying decorative before functional, then discovering on night two that there is no light and nothing to boil water in.

The seven, in the order to buy them

1. Rechargeable lamp or emergency light, GHS 80 to 150

First, before anything. An outage on your first night in an unfamiliar room is genuinely unpleasant, and a phone torch drains the phone you need. Look for one that also charges a phone.

2. Rechargeable fan, GHS 250 to 420

Second. Sleep matters more than everything below this line. Buy brushless if you can stretch to it, because it roughly doubles the hours you get from the same battery.

3. Electric kettle, GHS 110 to 230

The most-used appliance in most first homes. Tea, koko, gari, washing water, and hot water for cooking faster. A concealed element costs a little more and descales far more easily.

4. Hot plate or table top cooker, GHS 180 to 380

Single burner for one person, double if you will actually cook two things at once. This is the item people over-buy. A single burner and a little patience covers a first year comfortably.

5. Blender, GHS 280 to 340

Only if you cook properly rather than reheating. Get the commercial-style one with a dry mill if you grind pepper. If you eat out most nights, this can wait a month.

6. Pressing iron, GHS 150 to 200

You need to look presentable for work. A dry iron is cheaper, simpler, and safer across a mixed wardrobe.

7. Drying rack, GHS 150 to 200

Underrated. If you are in a flat with no yard, this is the difference between clean clothes and damp clothes that smell.

The total, honestly

Cheapest sensible version of all seven: about GHS 1,150. Better version, with a brushless fan and a 304 steel kettle: about GHS 1,500. The extra GHS 350 mostly buys years rather than features, and the two places it matters most are the fan motor and the kettle steel.

What can wait

Microwave, air fryer, standing fan, speaker, cookware sets. All pleasant, none urgent. A microwave in particular is a month-two purchase for most people, because a hot plate does everything it does with a little more time.

Two mistakes worth avoiding

Buying the biggest number. The blender claiming 8000W is not more powerful than the one claiming 600W. A Ghanaian socket cannot deliver either figure, and the number on the box is a peak marketing claim rather than what the motor draws.

Paying before delivery. On a first move you are spending most of what you have. Do not send money to anyone before you have the item in your hands and have checked it. Nobody honest requires it.

How to do this in one order

Start with the range, or message us with your budget and we will tell you honestly what to buy first.
